result.summary: Æneas sets up the trophy of Mezentius and sends Pallas home in a funeral procession, then grants the Latians a truce to bury their dead. In Latium, Diomede's refusal of help sets Drances against Turnus in council until news of the Trojan advance ends the debate. Camilla fights bravely and is killed by Arruns, and Diana's nymph Opis avenges her, after which the Latians flee to their walls and the two armies camp at nightfall.

scenes.title: Trophy of Mezentius
scenes.summary: Æneas dedicates Mezentius' arms to Mars and urges his men to bury the dead and send Pallas home.
scenes.stakes: The army's morale and the proper honouring of the fallen before the march on Latium.

scenes.title: Funeral procession for Pallas
scenes.summary: Æneas mourns over Pallas' body and the procession departs with spoils, captives and the weeping horse Æthon.
scenes.stakes: Æneas faces grief and his pledge to Evander, which he has failed to keep.

scenes.title: Truce with the Latians
scenes.summary: Latian envoys beg leave to bury their dead. Æneas agrees, and Drances praises him; a twelve-day truce follows.
scenes.stakes: The Latians risk further slaughter and the loss of their dead's burial rites.

scenes.title: Evander mourns Pallas
scenes.summary: Pallas' body reaches Pallanteum, and Evander laments and asks the Trojans to avenge his son by killing Turnus.
scenes.stakes: Evander has lost his only son and has only vengeance left.

scenes.title: Funeral pyres and Latian grief
scenes.summary: Both sides burn and bury their dead. In Latinus' city the mourners blame Turnus, and Drances presses the case against him.
scenes.stakes: Turnus' standing is threatened as the city turns against him.

scenes.title: Council summoned
scenes.summary: The embassy returns from Diomede with no help. Latinus convenes a council and calls on Venulus to report.

scenes.title: Diomede's refusal
scenes.summary: Venulus reports how Diomede in Arpi refused to fight, recounting the Greeks' sufferings and praising Æneas.
scenes.stakes: Diomede is wary of provoking the gods again and of facing Æneas.

scenes.title: Latinus proposes peace
scenes.summary: Latinus offers land and ships to the Trojans, and Drances demands Turnus yield and Lavinia be given to Æneas.
scenes.stakes: Turnus risks being forced to give up Lavinia, and Latium risks ruin.

scenes.title: Turnus answers Drances
scenes.summary: Turnus scorns Drances and accepts single combat. News of the advancing Trojans throws the city into uproar.
scenes.stakes: Turnus' honour and life are at risk, and so is the city under attack.

scenes.title: Preparations and Camilla's offer
scenes.summary: Turnus orders defences. The queen and matrons pray to Pallas, and Camilla offers to meet the cavalry while Turnus sets an ambush.
scenes.stakes: The city faces assault and Camilla's life is at stake.

scenes.title: Diana and Camilla's story
scenes.summary: Diana tells Opis how Camilla was saved as a baby by Metabus and consecrated to her, and sends Opis to avenge her.
scenes.stakes: Camilla's life is under a fated threat.

scenes.title: Cavalry battle and Camilla's feats
scenes.summary: The cavalry clash, and Camilla kills many Trojans and Tuscans, including the deceitful Ligurian son of Aunus.
scenes.stakes: Camilla risks her life and the Latians risk defeat.

scenes.title: Tarchon rallies; Arruns prays
scenes.summary: Tarchon rebukes the Tuscans and seizes Venulus. Arruns stalks Camilla and prays to Apollo, who grants only half the prayer.
scenes.stakes: Arruns hopes to kill Camilla and survive; Camilla is lured by spoils.

scenes.title: Death of Camilla and Arruns
scenes.summary: Arruns' spear kills Camilla, who sends Acca to Turnus. Opis shoots Arruns dead.
scenes.stakes: Camilla loses her life; Arruns is killed in vengeance.

scenes.title: Rout and nightfall
scenes.summary: The Latians flee to the gates and are slaughtered. Turnus leaves his ambush, Æneas passes through, and both armies camp at dusk.
scenes.stakes: Latium's city nearly falls, and Turnus abandons his ambush.

alias_notes.explanation: A title of Diana as goddess of the crossroads.
Epithet of Apollo, also used for the sun.
The Latian matrons' title for the goddess Pallas Athena, whose temple they pray in.

notable_quotes.reason: Æneas' farewell to Pallas, echoing the Roman funeral formula.
Epic apostrophe to Camilla, a classic Virgilian narrator's address.
Diomede names Æneas' piety as what sets him above Hector.

analysis.text: Grief and the cost of war dominate the book, from Pallas' funeral to Camilla's death, while Latium splits over whether to make peace.
The funeral rites, circling pyres and sacrificed captives reflect Roman funeral practice and the idea of piety. Camilla's story draws on Greek Amazon legends and Italian tradition.

legacy.text: Camilla became a model of the warrior maiden in later epics, notably Tasso's Clorinda in Jerusalem Delivered and Spenser's Britomart.
Dante recalls Camilla among the dead of Italy in the Inferno, who fell for the Latin land.

fun_facts.text: The line 'Æternum vale' in Æneas' farewell, rendered here as 'forever farewell', echoes Catullus' poem on his brother's grave.

language_notes.text: "Goddess of Dawn" is Aurora; "day-star" is the morning star or sun. The line marks the next morning after the battle.
"Hauberk" is a coat of mail, here Mezentius' body armour.
"Gallants" addresses the men as brave, spirited warriors.
Acheron is a river of the underworld, here standing for the realm of the dead; burial was thought to matter to the soul's rest.
"Ausonian" means Italian; Ausonia is a poetic name for Italy.
"Arbute" is the strawberry tree, whose pliant shoots are used to weave the bier.
"Teucrians" are the Trojans, named after their ancestor Teucer; "Tuscans" are the Etruscan allies; "Arcady" is Arcadia, Evander's homeland.
Olive boughs wrapped in wool were the traditional sign of suppliants asking for peace or mercy.
"Those who have left the sun" is a euphemism for the dead; "hosts" and "fathers of his bride" refer to Latinus and Lavinia's connection to Æneas.
"The War-god's die has fallen" compares the fortune of battle to a cast die; the dead's fate is settled.
"Withal bespeaks" means "at the same time addresses." "Boon" is a favour.
Æneas means the contest should have been settled by single combat, the survivor being whoever heaven or his own strength favoured.
"Kindle the flame beneath" means to light the funeral pyres for the dead.
The "walls of destiny" are the city fated to be founded by the Trojans in Italy, here called a new Troy.
"Wains" are wagons; "erst" means formerly.
Harbinger means a forerunner who announces what is coming. Fame is here a personified messenger, as elsewhere in the poem.
"Parts the breath of fields" means the line of torches cuts through the night air over the fields on either side of the road. The stray numbers are line markers.
Phrygians is a name for the Trojans, who came from Asia Minor. The translator uses it interchangeably with Trojans and Teucrians.
"Lets speech find her way": grief at last loosens his throat so he can speak. Speech is treated as a feminine figure.
"War-god" is Mars, here standing for war itself. Evander recalls Pallas promised to be cautious in battle.
"First-fruits" are the first produce of a harvest, offered to the gods. Here it means Pallas, the first yield of youth, lost in his first battle.
"My blessed spouse" is Evander's dead wife, Pallas' mother. He calls her fortunate for dying before this grief.
"Followed the friendly standards of Troy" means he wishes he had gone to war with Æneas and died, instead of sending his son.
"Hands we plighted" refers to the handshake that pledged the alliance between Evander and Æneas.
Teucrian means Trojan, from Teucer, an early Trojan king. Volscians were an Italian people fighting on Turnus' side.
"A giant trunk hung round with armour" pictures a trophy: a tree trunk dressed in a defeated enemy's armour. Evander says Turnus would be dead if Pallas were older.
"Owes the debt of Turnus' life": Æneas owes the killing of Turnus to Pallas and Evander, in return for their friendship and the death.
"Niche" means a place or role. Evander says only the killing of Turnus remains for Æneas' valour to fill.
The Goddess of Dawn is Aurora (the Greek Eos), the usual Roman way of marking daybreak.
"Thrice they ran their courses" describes a ritual circuit of the pyre by armed men and horsemen, a Roman funeral custom for honoured warriors.
"The weapons that sped so ill" means the arms that failed to save their owners or achieve victory.
"Promiscuous" here means mixed together without distinction, describing bodies burned in a heap.
"Casts his weight into the scale" means Drances adds his influence to tip the argument against Turnus.
"Lends him its shadow" means Queen Amata's reputation shelters and protects Turnus.
The hand that felled Ilion (Troy) is Diomede's; he was a leading Greek warrior at Troy.
Argyripa is the city later called Arpi in Apulia; Garganus is a headland there. Diomede settled in Italy after the war.
Saturn's reign refers to Italy's legendary golden age, when Saturn ruled Latium; Ausonia is a poetic name for Italy.
Minerva's baleful star, Eubœa's crags and Caphereus allude to the Greek fleet wrecked by storm on its voyage home, a punishment for the sack of Troy.
Proteus' pillars means Egypt, where Menelaus wandered; Ulysses' wanderings brought him to Sicily and the Cyclopes under Ætna.
Agamemnon, king of Mycenæ, was murdered on his return by his wife Clytemnestra and her lover Ægisthus (the adulterer).
Diomede's companions were said to have been turned into sea birds as punishment after he wounded Venus.
Dardanus was the Trojan ancestor; Inachus was the legendary first king of Argos. The sense is that Troy would have invaded Greece.
Ausonia is a poetic name for Italy; the sons of Ausonia are the Italians gathered in council.
"Seed of heaven" means descendants of the gods; the Trojans claim divine ancestry, notably through Venus, mother of Æneas.
Ætolian arms refers to Diomedes, the Greek hero settled in Italy, whose refusal to ally with the Latins was reported just before this scene.
Teucrians is another name for the Trojans, from their ancestor Teucer.
A talent was a large unit of weight, here of gold and ivory gifts.
The chair and striped robe are royal insignia, the curule chair and the trabea, symbols of kingship offered to the Trojans.
"Stars have set" is a figure for the deaths of Latin warriors.
"Give out to be your enemy" means you claim or proclaim me to be your enemy.
"Vantage-ground" means a position of safety and advantage; Turnus mocks Drances for shouting bravely only from behind the walls.
"Lodge the War-god" means to give Mars a home; Turnus sneers that Drances houses courage only in his tongue and fleeing feet.
Bitias and Pandarus were Trojan brothers, huge warriors who opened the gate to the Rutulians and were killed by Turnus in Book 9.
Turnus ironically says Greek heroes like Diomedes (Tydeus' son) and Achilles now fear Troy, and even the Aufidus, an Italian river, flees backward; these are mock-exaggerations of Drances' alarm.
"The Ætolian" is Diomedes, who settled at Arpi and refused to help the Latins when asked.
Camilla is the warrior maiden queen of the Volsci, who leads a cavalry force for Turnus.
Padusa is a marshy channel of the river Po, known for its swans.
"Wildered" means bewildered, confused and distraught by the grim crisis.
"Tritonian maiden" is Pallas (the Greek Athena), so called from Lake Triton or the river Triton, her reputed birthplace or haunt.
"Phrygian freebooter" is Æneas, called a Trojan (Phrygian) pirate by his enemies, who see him as a plundering foreigner.
"Champaign" means open, level country.
"Federate leaders" are the commanders of the allied forces.
"Jealous inlet" means an entrance so narrow it seems to guard the glen grudgingly.
Latona's daughter is Diana, goddess of the hunt and chastity; Opis is one of her attendant nymphs.
"Varying Casmilla" means he altered her mother's name slightly, so Casmilla became Camilla.
The Volscians were Camilla's people, the tribe that had driven out Metabus; Amasenus is a river in Latium.
"Cork-tree's forest bark" means bark of the cork oak, which is light and floats, used to wrap and protect the infant.
Trivia is a title of Diana, linked to crossroads and her triple nature (moon, hunt, underworld).
Instead of gold brooch and long mantle, she wears a tiger's skin hanging from her head down her back.
Strymon is a river in Thrace, where cranes were said to winter.
"Profane" here means violate by killing; Diana demands blood-payment from whoever slays her devotee.
"Champaign" means open, level country; here the plain where the battle is fought.
"Levinbolt" is an old word for a lightning bolt; the "engine" is a siege catapult.
Dian is Diana, goddess of the hunt, whose weapon is the bow; Camilla is her devotee, so her bow is Diana's "artillery".
Thermodon was the river of the Amazons; Hippolyte and Penthesilea were Amazon queens, the latter an ally of Troy in legend.
"Accoutred" means equipped or dressed; Iapygia is a region of south-eastern Italy known for horses.
"Rives" means splits or cleaves; "'twixt" is "betwixt", between.
"Bird of augury": hawks were watched by Romans as omens, so the bird carries prophetic weight.
The double negative means the scene is watched with full attention: Jupiter, the father of men and gods, sees everything from Olympus.
The Bacchic dance refers to the revels of Bacchus, god of wine. Tarchon taunts the Tuscans for eagerness in festivals but reluctance in battle.
Wry-necked fife: a pipe with a curved end, used in the worship of Bacchus.
Gripe means grip or clutch; pinions are wings.
Mæonia is an old name for Lydia in Asia Minor, from which the Etruscans were believed to have come; its sons here are the Tuscans.
The man of fate means Arruns is destined to be Camilla's killer.
Cybele was the Phrygian mother goddess, served by eunuch priests. Chloreus's Phrygian armour marks him as a Trojan ally.
Gortynian means from Gortyn in Crete, famed for archers; Lycian likewise names a land known for bows.
Soracte is a mountain north of Rome sacred to Apollo. The fire-walking rite was practised by his devotees, the Hirpi.
Vouchsafed means graciously granted; the last clause says the winds carried his words away unfulfilled.
The spear is 'heard' before it is seen; the Volscians' attention is drawn by its whistling flight, and 'centre' means the single point, the queen, they all look at.
'Caitiff' means a cowardly, wretched creature; 'wildered' means bewildered.
'Discumbers' is an archaic word meaning unburdens or frees herself, as from an encumbrance.
Trivia is a title of Diana, goddess of the hunt, associated with crossroads; Opis is her attendant nymph.
'Shent' is archaic for ruined or destroyed.
'Bestead' means helped or availed; the line says her service to Diana has not helped her.
'Guerdon' means reward or recompense, used here bitterly for the vengeance owed.
Thracian women were proverbially skilled warriors and archers, so the comparison fits a huntress goddess.
"Unnerved shoulders" means shoulders slack with fear, and the "unstrung bows" show the archers have abandoned fighting; "four-foot steeds" is a poetic phrase for galloping horses.
"As women wont to" means as women are accustomed to: the shriek is the traditional cry of women in distress.
"Whelmed" means overwhelmed or engulfed; "scape" is short for escape.
"Fain" means gladly or eagerly; "seared truncheons" are stakes hardened by fire.
"Jove's stern requirement" refers to the will of fate and the gods, which drives Turnus from his ambush toward his doom.
The "Hiberian flood" is the western ocean, where the sun-god Phœbus was imagined to unyoke his horses at sunset.

context_notes.text: Mars, the god of war, receives the trophy. Hanging a defeated enemy's armour on a tree or stake was a Roman custom.
Acœtes was Evander's old armour-bearer, sent to guard Pallas as a tutor and protector.
Dido, queen of Carthage, loved Æneas and then killed herself when he left; these cloaks are her gifts from that earlier time.
Captives killed at a funeral as offerings to the dead man's spirit follow Homeric precedent, recalling Achilles at Patroclus' pyre.
Drances is a Latin elder and rival of Turnus; earlier in Book 11 he openly blames Turnus for the war.
The truce allows both sides to gather wood for the funeral pyres, hence the felling of trees that follows.
Evander is the Arcadian king of Pallanteum, on the future site of Rome. He sent his son Pallas to fight beside Æneas.
Funeral processions were held by torchlight, and torches were carried to escort the dead.
The Tyrrhene leaders are the Etruscans, who had allied themselves with Æneas against Turnus.
Turnus, king of the Rutulians, killed Pallas in single combat and took his sword belt, which matters later in the poem.
Tarchon is the Etruscan leader allied with Æneas against Turnus and the Latians.
"Turnus' bridal rites" refers to his claim to marry Lavinia, the cause of the war.
Drances is an envious Latian nobleman and Turnus' bitter political rival, who opposes him in council.
Diomede, a Greek hero at Troy, settled in Italy; the Latins had sent envoys asking him to join them against the Trojans.
In the Iliad Diomede wounded Venus (Aphrodite), Æneas' mother, as she rescued her son in battle.
Æneas is regularly marked by piety (devotion to gods and duty), the virtue that defines him in the poem.
The land lies along the Tiber (the Tuscan river), offered as a settlement for the Trojans.
Drances is a wealthy Latin noble and Turnus's political rival, shown here as a talker rather than a fighter.
The gift Drances adds is Lavinia, the king's daughter, promised to Turnus but destined for Æneas.
Evander was the Arcadian king allied with Æneas; his son Pallas was slain by Turnus in Book 10, and Turnus boasts of that victory.
Vulcan, god of the forge, made Æneas' divine armour at the request of Venus.
The royal father-in-law is King Latinus, whose daughter Lavinia Turnus hopes to marry.
Latinus is king of Latium. He had promised Lavinia to Æneas, then gave way to Turnus' claim, and he now regrets rejecting the Trojans' offer.
Lavinia is Latinus' daughter, the bride over whom Turnus and Æneas are fighting.
Camilla is a warrior maiden of the Volsci, who leads their cavalry in support of Turnus.
Metabus was king of Privernum, driven out by his subjects for tyranny; Camilla later leads Volscian cavalry for Turnus.
Tyrrhene means Etruscan; many Italian mothers wished Camilla to marry their sons, but she stays a virgin huntress.
Diana promises to rescue Camilla's body and return it to her homeland, foretelling that Camilla will die.
The Trojans and their Etruscan (Tuscan) allies under Aeneas' side approach Latium's city, where Latin horsemen meet them.
Camilla is a Volscian warrior maiden, dedicated since childhood to Diana, who fights like the legendary Amazons.
Ligurians, from north-west Italy, had a reputation among the Romans for cunning and deceit.
Jupiter takes an interest in the battle and spurs Tarchon, the Etruscan leader allied with Aeneas, to action.
Arruns is an Etruscan fighting with the Latins. He prays to Apollo to be allowed to kill Camilla, the Volscian warrior maiden.
Arruns says he seeks no spoils, only to remove the shame of Camilla's slaughter of men. He will come home without honour.
Acca is Camilla's close companion among the women warriors of her band, and the one she trusts with her last message.
Teucrians are the Trojans; Tyrrhenes are the Etruscans, allies of Aeneas, and Evander's Arcadians are his Greek-descended cavalry from Pallanteum.
Dercennus was an old king of Laurentum, the Latin territory; his burial mound serves as Opis's vantage point.
Camilla was the Volscian warrior-maiden, killed in the preceding fighting; the Rutulians are Turnus' people. Latians and Rutulians are allied against the Trojans.
Acca is Camilla's companion, who brings Turnus the news. Turnus had been lying in ambush in a wooded pass to trap Æneas.
Laurentum was the Latin city of King Latinus; "Teucrians" and Æneas' men are the Trojans.

literary_notes.text: Æneas addresses the dead boy directly, and Fortune is personified as one who has grudged Pallas to him, heightening the grief.
Evander is still hopefully making vows and offerings, unaware his son is dead, while the reader and Æneas know.
Pallas is compared to a cut flower that keeps its colour though severed from the earth, conveying fragile beauty and untimely death.
Æthon the warhorse weeps as if he shared human grief, showing how deeply the loss is felt.
The repeated "forever" in the farewell echoes the Roman funeral formula of final parting.
The epithet "good" and his readiness to grant the prayer present Æneas as merciful and just.
Drances's extravagant praise, matching Æneas "with the stars," also shows his flattery and his hostility toward Turnus.
The ash "rings" and the wains "groan," giving the forest and carts voices that convey the busy work.
Fame is a winged figure who flies and fills ears with tidings, making rumour an active agent of grief.
Fame earlier hailed Pallas as victor, so the same voice now brings the opposite news, sharpening the reversal.
The long line of torches gleaming through the dark fields makes the funeral march vivid and sets mourning against night.
Evander's remark that he knew the lure of first glory shows his earlier fear, which the death has now confirmed.
Evander cries out to his dead wife and to Pallas, who cannot hear, conveying his raw grief through repeated "alas".
He turns to address Turnus, his absent enemy, so that the speech moves from grief toward threat.
Evander refuses glory or triumph and asks only for news to bring to Pallas in the underworld, showing a father's grief and restraint.
Dark smoke veiling the sky in gloom conveys the scale of the burning and the mood of mourning.
Repeating "sprinkled" at the start of each clause stresses how pervasive the weeping is.
Honoured burial for some and uncounted, unhonoured burning for others sharpens the sense of Latian loss.
The narrator shifts from the battlefield to the city, concentrating the grief among those left behind.
The 'blaze of popular turmoil' pictures the crowd's anger as a fire at its height, intensifying the blow of the failed embassy.
Diomede addresses the Latins as 'children of fortune', ironically calling them lucky while warning them of the war's cost.
His outcry against the 'cruel gods' conveys personal grief and bitterness at his lost home and wife.
The 'whirlwind' of Æneas' lance turns the weapon into a storm, showing the force Diomede has felt firsthand.
Diomede's judgment sets Æneas above Hector through piety, defining the Trojan hero by moral quality rather than strength alone.
The murmuring assembly is compared to a river checked by rocks, its sound rising from the pent-up water.
A string of contrasts, bold in speech but feeble in battle, rich but obscure on his father's side, sketches Drances before he speaks.
"Danger's throat" and "wellspring of ills" portray Turnus as the source of Latium's troubles and war as a devouring mouth.
Drances uses indignant questioning to portray ordinary Latins as sacrificed for Turnus's marriage prospects.
Turnus sarcastically credits Drances with the slaughter of Trojans, when in fact Drances has done nothing but talk.
Turnus exaggerates the effect of Drances' speeches to ridicule them, as if they dwarf the army and terrify nations.
Fortune is shown as a playful figure who tosses men about and then sets them on a rock.
The noise of the frightened crowd is compared to flocks of birds and hoarse swans, conveying chaotic, loud confusion.
Lavinia's downcast eyes show her quiet shame and helplessness as the unwilling cause of war.
Turnus is likened to a spirited horse breaking free, conveying his eager, exuberant confidence and his vigour.
The "treacherous forest" ambush hints at danger and deceit to come in the battle.
Metabus's hesitation shows tender paternal love, softening the hard exile described as wild and untamed.
The epithet "poor Camilla" and the image of the infant flying on a spear evoke pity and danger.
The mare's milk and savage lairs depict Camilla's wild, unnatural upbringing apart from human society.
Diana's wish that Camilla had never gone to war hints at her coming death.
Opis's swift descent, wrapped in a black whirlwind, gives the goddess's messenger a stormlike, ominous quality.
Missiles falling "thick as snow-flakes" conveys the density of the volley and darkens the sky.
The advancing and retreating tide mirrors the back-and-forth surge of the Latian and Trojan cavalry.
The narrator addresses Camilla directly, heightening drama before the catalogue of her victims.
Camilla offers the dying man a bitter consolation, glory from being killed by a woman, after mocking his boasts.
Camilla's taunt ties the son's deceit to his father, Aunus the liar, making treachery a family trait.
The hawk and dove image shows Camilla's swift, predatory kill and the helplessness of her victim.
Tarchon's speed is likened to lightning, stressing the sudden violence of the abduction.
The eagle and serpent extend the struggle of Tarchon and Venulus, with the eagle's calm control mirroring Tarchon's triumph.
Arruns' silent, patient stalking shows him as cunning and cold, in contrast with Camilla's open daring.
Camilla's blind hunter's greed for plunder shows the weakness that will expose her to Arruns' dart.
Apollo grants Arruns only half of his prayer: Camilla will die, but he will never come home.
Arruns's mix of joy and fear shows him to be a petty man, unlike the proud warrior he has just killed.
Arruns's furtive flight is compared to a wolf that has killed and slinks away, tail tucked, showing his guilty cowardice.
Her soul resents its lot and flies groaning, as in the Aeneid's other heroic deaths, giving the death a tragic bitterness.
Opis's mocking question reveals that Arruns's escape was an illusion; he is doomed by the goddess whose follower he killed.
The repeated "flies... fly... flies" mimics the panic and spreading rout of the fleeing troops.
Men reach their native walls, the place of safety, only to die on the threshold.
The matrons' fierce improvised defense shows civic devotion, echoing Camilla's warrior spirit.
The sun as Phœbus bathing his tired horses turns nightfall into a gentle image that halts the battle.
